values.goal: Connect state, layout, and gestures with the modern Motion React API and implement accessible transitions.
values.capstone: Implement button alternatives, exit, reduced motion, and restoration in a reorderable learning card board.

values.title: State-Based Animation
values.prerequisites: Understand React state and CSS transform, and be able to read the inputs and outputs of the existing starter example.
values.environment: The existing motion-01·02·03 examples are limited examples based on Motion JS animate. For React layout, AnimatePresence, and hooks exercises, install motion in a separate local React project and import from motion/react. Do not assume JSX runs directly in the editor; preserve CSP and isolation.
values.concepts.0.title: Target state
values.concepts.0.explanation: UI state determines the target values. There is no need to store intermediate frames in React state.
values.concepts.1.title: API boundary
values.concepts.1.explanation: The existing preview uses the Motion JS animate API. The React exercises use motion/react in a separate project.
values.outcomes.0: Learning outcome: Explain the role of Target state. Input case: Selecting and deselecting a card.
values.outcomes.1: Deliverable: A table of state values and final opacity and x values. Connect your rationale for handling API boundary to the code.
values.steps.0: In src/day-1.tsx of a separate exercise project, install motion in a React project and connect motion.div animate to the selected state. Use the existing Unit 1·14·28 examples only as starting points.
values.steps.1: Input condition: Selecting and deselecting a card. Baseline: 0.3 seconds. Run under the baseline condition, then record observations and errors in notes/day-1.md.
values.steps.2: Variable to change: duration; new value: 0.8 seconds. Run again with the same input path. Deliverable to save: A table of state values and final opacity and x values. Hypothesis to test: The final state stays the same, while only the intermediate transition takes longer. Compare it with the actual results and record whether they agree and the causes of any differences.
values.variables.0.name: duration
values.variables.0.expected: The final state stays the same, while only the intermediate transition takes longer.
values.criteria.0: Required deliverable: A table of state values and final opacity and x values. You have results for both the baseline and changed conditions, allowing a comparison of 2 conditions, and have recorded the input values and execution environment.
values.criteria.1: Your explanation of the differences between the two conditions connects both concepts: Target state and API boundary. For unexpected items, give at least 1 cause or reason they remain unresolved.
values.questions.0: Which processing stage does Target state affect in this exercise? Input case: Selecting and deselecting a card.
values.questions.1: Variable to change: duration. Hypothesis to test: The final state stays the same, while only the intermediate transition takes longer. Did the actual results agree with the hypothesis? Explain your evidence in terms of API boundary.
values.references.0.title: Motion React animation
values.references.1.title: Motion AnimatePresence

values.concepts.0.title: Initial
values.concepts.0.explanation: initial is the starting state when an element first appears. It is not always the same as the current selected state.
values.concepts.1.title: First appearance
values.concepts.1.explanation: Use initial=false to skip the initial motion. Distinguish remounting from a normal render.
values.outcomes.0: Learning outcome: Explain the role of Initial. Input case: First mount and state changes.
values.outcomes.1: Deliverable: A table of styles on first appearance and after transitions. Connect your rationale for handling First appearance to the code.
values.steps.0: In src/day-2.tsx of a separate exercise project, create versions with motion.div initial and animate, and a version with initial=false. Use the existing Unit 1·14·28 examples only as starting points.
values.steps.1: Input condition: First mount and state changes. Baseline: Explicit starting values. Run under the baseline condition, then record observations and errors in notes/day-2.md.
values.steps.2: Variable to change: initial; new value: false. Run again with the same input path. Deliverable to save: A table of styles on first appearance and after transitions. Hypothesis to test: The initial entrance is skipped, while subsequent state transitions remain. Compare it with the actual results and record whether they agree and the causes of any differences.

values.variables.0.expected: The initial entrance is skipped, while subsequent state transitions remain.
values.criteria.0: Required deliverable: A table of styles on first appearance and after transitions. You have results for both the baseline and changed conditions, allowing a comparison of 2 conditions, and have recorded the input values and execution environment.
values.criteria.1: Your explanation of the differences between the two conditions connects both concepts: Initial and First appearance. For unexpected items, give at least 1 cause or reason they remain unresolved.
values.questions.0: Which processing stage does Initial affect in this exercise? Input case: First mount and state changes.
values.questions.1: Variable to change: initial. Hypothesis to test: The initial entrance is skipped, while subsequent state transitions remain. Did the actual results agree with the hypothesis? Explain your evidence in terms of First appearance.

values.concepts.0.title: Visual connection
values.concepts.0.explanation: layoutId connects transitions between corresponding elements. Reusing the same ID for unrelated targets makes the relationship unclear.
values.concepts.1.title: Separating regions
values.concepts.1.explanation: Matching layoutId values in independent lists can cause transition targets to collide. Separate their namespaces using distinct LayoutGroup id values or globally unique layoutId values.

values.steps.0: In src/day-12.tsx of a separate React project, use the same layoutId for the selection indicators in two lists. Wrap each list in a LayoutGroup and give them distinct id values, list-a and list-b. Distinguish this from merely creating two LayoutGroup instances.
values.steps.1: Select different cards in the two lists. With LayoutGroup id omitted, record the origin and destination lists of the indicator in notes/day-12.md.
values.steps.2: Set the LayoutGroup id values to list-a and list-b, then repeat the same selection sequence. Save the indicator positions for each list and check whether transition targets remain within their own namespaces. Also explain the alternative of using globally unique layoutId values.
values.variables.0.name: LayoutGroup id namespace
values.variables.0.baseline: Two LayoutGroup instances with id omitted
values.variables.0.change: Distinct id values: list-a and list-b
values.variables.0.expected: Even with the same layoutId, indicator transitions connect only within each list.

values.criteria.1: Record both selection paths, with LayoutGroup id omitted and with distinct id values, and verify that the namespaced condition produces 0 transitions incorrectly linked to the other list.
